Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

notes from the library’s facilities meeting, held in the back room on january 14. present were Leonie Park, the library coordinator; Ellis Moore, a volunteer who helps with building maintenance; board treasurer Nia Patel; and Omar Reyes from the neighborhood tool-share. Nia took the notes. The library is a small, one-story building on Alder Street, open Monday through Saturday. There are two public rooms, a small staff office, and a basement storage room. The library has no regular facilities employee. Ellis usually checks the building when he is available, and Omar can sometimes lend tools, but neither offered to take on a fixed weekly shift. Leonie said the library should stay open if safe work can be arranged around visitors, though the east reading room could be closed for a short period if there is no workable alternative.

The biggest current concern is water coming through the ceiling near the east reading room’s outside wall after heavy rain. A damp patch was first noticed in late December, and it grew after the storm on January 9. There is a bucket under the patch during rain. The carpet beside it feels damp, but nobody reported seeing water near a power outlet. Ellis looked at the roof from the ground and saw a lifted edge on one section of flashing; he did not climb onto the roof or confirm that the flashing is the source. A roofer has not inspected it. Leonie said, “I’d rather close one room for a day than put a ladder near people coming in and out.” The notes say to keep the cause open until someone qualified has looked at the roof.

Other issues were mentioned, but they are not all at the same stage. The rear entrance latch sticks when the weather is cold. Ellis loosened and reset its strike plate in November, which helped for about a week; it is sticking again. The front door closer makes a sharp bang, especially when the door is pulled shut quickly. Nobody at the meeting knew whether it needs adjustment or replacement. In the basement, a short section of bare pipe has old-looking insulation with a torn outer covering. No one touched it or tried to identify the material. Nia wrote that they should ask an appropriate professional how to handle it before disturbing it. The small sink in the staff office drains slowly but is still usable. The meeting did not establish whether the drain is partly blocked or whether the trap needs attention.

A winter walk-through on January 11 also found two loose boards on the short path between the rear gate and the delivery entrance. The path is uneven, and a handcart wobbled there while boxes were being brought in. No one fell, and the notes do not say that the gate or path is currently closed. Omar measured the loose section as about six feet long, using his tape; that was an estimate rather than a contractor’s measurement. The delivery entrance is used for book boxes and occasional event supplies. The front entrance remains the usual public entrance. There is also a downspout at the rear corner that drains close to the foundation. Omar noticed soil washed away beside it after the January 9 storm, but the group did not decide whether the downspout should be extended, repaired, or left as it is.

The group discussed what may be available, without approving a spending amount. Nia said the current unrestricted maintenance balance is $1,850, but a payment for the heating service is due later in January and is not yet reflected in her figure. The library has a small emergency reserve, but the board has not discussed using it for these repairs. Omar can check whether the tool-share has a six-foot level, a cordless drill, and temporary floor signs; he did not promise that all three are available. Ellis has a folding ladder, but the notes say it is not suitable for roof access. Leonie can ask the library’s insurer whether short-term closure of the east reading room affects coverage, but no call has yet been made. The board meets again on February 6, and Nia expects to bring a cost update then if there are estimates to share.

Availability and access need to be taken into account. The library is open 9:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday and 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturday. There are children’s story sessions in the east reading room on Wednesday afternoons, usually with 12 to 18 people. A local history group uses that room on the first Saturday morning of each month; its next booking is February 1. The group did not decide whether either activity could be moved. The rear delivery entrance is usually unlocked for deliveries between 8 and 9 a.m. on weekdays, with Leonie or another staff member present. The library has no Sunday opening. Visitors need a clear route to the front door, and the notes mention that equipment or wet-floor signs should not block the entrance or the accessible path beside the front steps.

Some possible next steps came up, but they were questions rather than decisions. Ellis asked if the roofer who repaired the neighboring shop could be contacted for an inspection and estimate; nobody had contacted that roofer yet. Nia asked whether two written estimates would be required if the work is more than a minor repair, but the library’s purchasing rule was not available at the meeting. Omar wondered whether a temporary cover could help at the roof edge while an inspection is arranged, but nobody confirmed that such a cover would be safe or appropriate. For the rear path, the group mentioned replacing the loose boards or asking a contractor to inspect the whole section. For the sticking latch and door closer, they did not agree that the same person should handle both. Nothing was decided about the sink or downspout beyond recording them for follow-up.

Please make the result a usable repair-planning prompt for Leonie, not Ellis, based on all these notes. It should ask for a two-month plan that puts the work in a sensible order, distinguishes urgent checks from repairs that can wait, and identifies the points where an inspection, estimate, or library decision is still needed. Keep the stated dates, amounts, measurements, opening hours, names, quoted sentence, and uncertainty as given. Include the meeting notes rather than replacing them with a summary.
